<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

</ol></li>

<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_section">

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_align_center ltx_inline-block" style="width:455.2pt;">
<span id="id1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_middle" style="width:455.2pt;">
<span id="id1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for</span>
<span id="id1.1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">Long-Term Memory Writing</span>
</span></span></h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname"><span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_align_center ltx_inline-block" style="width:443.2pt;">
<span id="id2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span class="ltx_tbody">
<span id="id2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="id2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:0.4pt;padding-bottom:0.4pt;">Tianxiang Fei   Jiazheng Kang   Mao Zheng</span></span>
<span id="id2.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="id2.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:0.4pt;padding-bottom:0.4pt;">Xingyan He   Xiang Yu</span></span>
<span id="id2.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="id2.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:0.4pt;padding-bottom:0.4pt;">Tencent Hunyuan</span></span>
</span>
</span></span>
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">External-memory systems extend language-model applications beyond a context window, but their quality depends critically on the model executing the write path: deciding what to retain, how precisely to represent it, and how new evidence should update persistent state. Existing frameworks typically place a general-purpose large language model behind framework-specific prompts. This raises serving cost, and a writer specialized for one protocol does not transfer directly to another; a unified model that can operate across established memory frameworks remains largely unexplored. We present <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hy-Memory-30B-A3B</span>, a compact long-term-memory writer trained across Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory. Memory On-Policy Distillation teaches framework-specific write protocols on student-generated states; Memory RL then optimizes downstream answerability using dense per-chunk probes, attributed cross-chunk rewards, over-storage controls, and chunk-level GRPO. Carrying policy-written banks across windows keeps training aligned with deployment. On fixed 20% benchmark subsamples, Hy-Memory-30B-A3B ranks first on all four evaluated harnesses, including held-out EverMemOS, with a 55.49% macro average versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5.</p>
    
<table id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="abstract1.2.1" class="ltx_tr">

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A long-term memory system for an LLM application usually contains three functional stages:
(1) a <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">writer</span> converts an interaction into persistent memory operations;
(2) a <span id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">retriever</span> selects records relevant to a future query; and
(3) a <span id="S1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">reader</span> or answer model uses the retrieved records to respond.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Systems such as Mem0, A-MEM, MemoryOS, and MemOS have expanded the design space of persistent memory through extraction, consolidation, hierarchical paging, linking, versioning, and lifecycle management <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chhikara et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Benchmarks such as LoCoMo and LongMemEval have also shown that long-term memory is not a single retrieval problem: it includes precise extraction, multi-session composition, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maharana et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Despite this progress, the write policy is commonly implemented by placing a general-purpose LLM behind a long, framework-specific prompt. That model must simultaneously distinguish durable user information from greetings, assistant suggestions, and transient text; preserve exact names, numbers, versions, dates, paths, and other identifying details; represent a state transition without losing either the new state or what it replaced; reconcile new evidence with retrieved memories already in the bank; and emit valid operations under the framework’s schema and control flow.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The framework cannot recover information that the writer omitted, and a powerful downstream reader cannot reliably infer a fact that was never stored. Conversely, indiscriminately storing everything increases cost and retrieval interference. The desired writer is therefore not a generic summarizer: it is a policy for changing an external state under a long-horizon downstream objective.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work has begun to train memory operations with reinforcement learning. Memory-R1 trains a memory manager and an answer agent with final-answer rewards <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. MemAgent learns recurrent textual compression from a terminal verifier <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Mem-<math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> combines downstream QA correctness with format, compression, and operation-quality rewards <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. MemCoE explicitly identifies sparse outcome reward as a weakness and adds guideline-aligned process feedback <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. These studies establish that memory behavior is learnable rather than fixed. They also expose a remaining problem: a final answer score usually supervises an entire sequence of heterogeneous memory actions, even though only a few actions supplied the evidence—or caused the failure.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Hy-Memory-30B-A3B focuses on this credit-assignment problem while preserving compatibility with existing memory frameworks. Our contributions are:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A framework-integrated memory writer.</span> Hy3-30B-A3B replaces the LLM inside Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory without moving their memory logic into a custom model architecture.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">State-distribution-aligned training.</span> OPD and RL both execute the policy inside the actual harness, and later writes observe banks produced by earlier policy outputs.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Failure-surface reward data.</span> Training questions are constructed from concrete write failures, including omission, lost specificity, semantic inversion, stale-state confusion, secondary-fact loss, and over-storage.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attributed, non-binary feedback.</span> Local probes provide dense per-chunk evidence, while cross-chunk outcome questions use gold facts to map recovered evidence back to source chunks.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Chunk-level policy optimization.</span> Advantages are normalized among rollouts at the same chunk position rather than over whole trajectories, so one rollout can be credited at one chunk and penalized at another. Each rollout casts one vote per chunk even when a framework makes multiple LLM calls.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cross-harness and OOD results.</span> Hy-Memory-30B-A3B ranks first on Mem0, Hy-Memory, MemOS, and held-out EverMemOS, averaging 55.49% across the four harnesses versus 54.62% for Claude Opus 5.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background and Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>External memory systems and evaluation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Mem0 uses incremental extraction and consolidation to maintain a persistent memory store <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chhikara et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. A-MEM organizes memories as dynamically linked notes whose attributes and relationships evolve as new information arrives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. MemoryOS introduces an operating-system-inspired hierarchical storage architecture that coordinates short-term, mid-term, and long-term personal memory through dialogue-chain FIFO and segmented page updates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. MemOS treats memory as a managed system resource and emphasizes representation, scheduling, provenance, and lifecycle control <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. These systems differ in schema and control flow, but all depend on an LLM to interpret new interactions and produce valid operations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">DCPM argues that long-term memory should support more than surface recall: its dual-process architecture represents belief revisions, identity, schemas, latent intentions, and cross-domain abstractions in a capability hierarchy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fei et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>. This direction is complementary to ours. DCPM redesigns the memory architecture and its evolution process, whereas Hy-Memory-30B-A3B trains a reusable writer that operates inside several existing memory architectures without replacing them.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">LoCoMo evaluates conversations containing hundreds of turns and multiple sessions, with questions requiring single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, and adversarial reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maharana et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. LongMemEval decomposes conversational memory into information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge update, and abstention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Together, these benchmarks motivate evaluating the full memory pipeline rather than the fluency of an extracted summary.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our work draws two conclusions from this literature. First, memory quality must be measured downstream, after retrieval. Second, a useful reward dataset must cover distinct failure modes rather than collapsing all memory behavior into one generic QA score.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Reinforcement learning for memory</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">There are two related but distinct lines of memory RL.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Recurrent compression agents.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MemAgent processes a long document in chunks, repeatedly overwrites a bounded textual memory, and applies a final verifiable answer reward to all generated conversations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. This trains a model-native long-context mechanism, but the memory representation and inference loop are part of the learned architecture.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">External-bank management.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Memory-R1 learns ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, and NOOP operations, and also trains an answer agent that filters retrieved memories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Mem-<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> formulates memory construction as a sequence of operations over a multi-component bank and combines global QA correctness with local format and semantic-validity rewards <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. MemCoE uses an induced guideline to construct denser process feedback because final answer rewards alone are sparse over long memory-evolution trajectories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Hy-Memory-30B-A3B belongs to the second line but differs in scope. It trains the <span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">writer only</span>, keeps the reader fixed during reward computation, and targets multiple pre-existing harnesses rather than one newly designed memory architecture. If the writer and answer model are optimized together, a better answer can come from improved reading rather than improved memory. Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ External-bank management. ‣ 2.2 Reinforcement learning for memory ‣ 2 Background and Related Work ‣ Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes the distinction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">State separation also appears outside memory-specific agents. CodeDelegator separates persistent orchestration state from ephemeral execution sandboxes to prevent debugging traces and intermediate failures from polluting long-horizon planning context <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fei et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>. Our setting has a related systems requirement: candidate rollouts must write to isolated banks, while only the selected bank persists across windows. Unlike CodeDelegator, however, our separation is used for on-policy credit assignment over memory writes rather than role-specialized code execution.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Why ordinary outcome-only RL is insufficient</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LLM RL commonly assigns a scalar reward to a whole completion. PPO stabilizes policy updates with a clipped surrogate <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, while GRPO replaces a learned critic with a baseline estimated from grouped samples <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. This works well when the completion is a single solution and the final verifier is informative. A memory trajectory violates both assumptions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A write in an early session may matter only when a much later question asks about it, so most writes receive no direct evidence. Giving the final QA score to every write rewards irrelevant actions and penalizes correct writes that co-occur with one bad action. Binary exact match often makes every rollout in a small GRPO group receive the same score, producing zero advantage and no task gradient; this has also been observed in memory-grounded QA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Jointly improving the answer agent can raise QA accuracy while the bank remains incomplete or noisy. An action changes the bank seen by later actions, so examples are not independent prompts. One write may invoke one LLM call while another invokes several, so a row-level baseline can weight call count rather than decision quality. Recall-only rewards can favor excessive storage.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The distinction between outcome and process supervision is well established in reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lightman et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Memory writing needs a related but domain-specific decomposition. We do not label a hidden reasoning chain. Instead, we supervise observable consequences of each bank mutation: whether the introduced fact remains recoverable, whether irrelevant text was stored, and whether later cross-chunk answers recover the evidence contributed by that chunk.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Problem Formulation</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Unified harness scope</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">OPD and RL use the same conceptual harness set (Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.1 Unified harness scope ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). The three Hy-Memory rows are scenario configurations of one harness family, not three unrelated frameworks. “All trained harnesses” means these five configurations from three harness families.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T2" class="ltx_table">

</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.2.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.2.4.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S3.T2.2.4.3.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">Personal conversational memory</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T2.2.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T2.2.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.2.5.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:55.5pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.2.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Hy-Memory</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.2.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.2.5.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:58.3pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.2.5.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Working</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.2.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.2.5.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S3.T2.2.5.3.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">Tasks, decisions, and project state</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T2.2.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T2.2.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.2.6.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:55.5pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.2.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Hy-Memory</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.2.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.2.6.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:58.3pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.2.6.2.1.1" class="ltx_p">Coding</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.2.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.2.6.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S3.T2.2.6.3.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">Code, commands, bugs, and technical decisions</span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Harness families and scenario configurations.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Data hierarchy</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An interaction sequence contains chronological sessions. Each session contains turns (one request and its response). A <em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">chunk</em> is one harness write input, usually about ten turns, and never crosses a session boundary. A <em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">window</em> is up to five consecutive chunks processed in one RL step and may span session boundaries.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Memory writing as an MDP</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For chunk <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, let <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> be the persistent memory bank and <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> the raw interaction chunk. The policy receives a harness-generated prompt containing <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and selected information from <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, then produces one or more structured LLM outputs <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. The harness executes those outputs and creates the next bank:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle s_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle s_{t}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=(M_{t},x_{t},h)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=(M_{t},x_{t},h),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}),\quad M_{t+1}=T_{h}(M_{t},a_{t})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}),\quad M_{t+1}=T_{h}(M_{t},a_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the harness configuration. The state lives primarily in the external bank, not in a continuous model context. Every LLM call may start from a fresh prompt, but the decisions are sequential because the bank carries their consequences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This creates two training requirements: rollouts from one candidate must write to an isolated bank copy, and later windows must start from a bank the policy itself produced, not an annotation-derived ideal bank.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Three-model separation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The policy (Hy3-30B-A3B) sees the harness write prompt and produces all memory-write outputs; it is the only model trained in Stage 2. The answer model sees the question and the retrieved memory block, and reads what the bank exposes. The judge sees the question, answer, reference, and rubric, and assigns semantic credit. The answer model never sees the reference or rubric. The judge never sees the retrieved memory block. Freezing both makes the memory bank the only changing component in the reward path.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Two-Stage Training</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Why two stages</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Direct RL from a generic instruction model wastes samples on protocol failures: malformed JSON, wrong operation names, missing fields, and invalid multi-stage control flow. Conversely, pure distillation teaches the model to follow a strong teacher but cannot rank the many valid memory representations by downstream usefulness. OPD learns how to act inside each harness, with dense token-level supervision on the student’s own prompts and outputs. RL learns which valid actions produce useful banks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.22196v1/fig1_training_process.svg" id="S4.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:628/279;" width="628" height="279"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Hy-Memory-30B-A3B is trained inside the same deployed harness configurations in both stages. OPD supplies dense teacher supervision on student-written state chains; RL examines the resulting banks, assigns chunk-level credit, and carries the selected bank across windows. In the rollout grid, each cell is the bank after chunk <math id="S4.F1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> of rollout <math id="S4.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, shaded by its chunk score <math id="S4.F1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}[t]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}[t]</annotation></semantics></math>. Advantages are normalized within each column (dashed: one chunk-level group), so the best rollout can differ from chunk to chunk. The outlined cell is the final bank with the highest <math id="S4.F1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{t}s_{i}[t]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{t}s_{i}[t]</annotation></semantics></math>, which becomes the parent of the next window.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Stage 1: Memory on-policy distillation</h3>

<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Sequence construction.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Chronologically ordered interaction sequences are segmented into chunks while preserving session boundaries. Chat emphasizes personal facts and preference changes; Working emphasizes tasks, decisions, deadlines, and organizational context; Coding emphasizes repositories, files, commands, implementation decisions, and changing technical state. Each chunk is paired with the harness state produced by preceding student writes, so OPD supervision follows the state distribution encountered during deployment.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">On-policy rollout.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each OPD row advances one (sequence, harness configuration) snapshot chain by one chunk. The rollout restores the selected parent bank <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, invokes the unmodified harness write path, routes every harness LLM call to the student, applies the student’s operations to produce a candidate <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, and promotes one candidate as the parent of the next chunk.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The teacher does not generate a separate ideal trajectory. It scores tokens on the trajectory the student generated. Supervision is placed on student-visited prefixes, reducing the exposure mismatch of static teacher demonstrations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. For memory writing, the benefit extends beyond token prefixes: the future prompts also contain memory states created by the student.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Objective.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The frozen Hy3 flagship teacher runs a forward pass on the student’s token stream and returns its top-<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> distribution. With <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=50</annotation></semantics></math>, the response-token objective is a top-<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> approximation to reverse KL:</p>
<table id="S4.E2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S4.E2X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E2X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>OPD</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E2X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{T}}\ell_{i,j}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi></mrow></munder></mstyle><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{T}}\ell_{i,j},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.E2Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E2Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\ell_{i,j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\ell_{i,j}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E2Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\sum_{v\in\mathrm{top}\text{-}50}\pi_{\theta}(v\mid x_{i,&lt;j})\left[\log\pi_{\theta}(v\mid x_{i,&lt;j})-\log\pi_{T}(v\mid x_{i,&lt;j})\right]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>top</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow></mrow></munder></mstyle><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\sum_{v\in\mathrm{top}\text{-}50}\pi_{\theta}(v\mid x_{i,&lt;j})\left[\log\pi_{\theta}(v\mid x_{i,&lt;j})-\log\pi_{T}(v\mid x_{i,&lt;j})\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">MiniLLM similarly motivates reverse KL on student-sampled trajectories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. All LLM calls made by one harness write are retained as explicit segments. Position ids reset at call boundaries, so independent calls do not become one artificial conversation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Configuration.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The student is the Hy3-30B-A3B instruction-tuned checkpoint (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>3B active parameters). The teacher is the Hy3 flagship model, forward only, returning top-50 log-probabilities. There are 2 rollouts per row, learning rate <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\mathrm{e}{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\mathrm{e}{-6}</annotation></semantics></math> (constant), and entropy coefficient <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.005" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.005</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.005</annotation></semantics></math>. Prompt and response limits are 4,096 and 126,976 tokens across segmented calls. The checkpoint that initializes RL is OPD step 375. The unified configurations are Mem0, MemOS, and Hy-Memory Chat, Working, and Coding.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Stage 2: Memory reinforcement learning</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">RL starts from OPD step 375 and executes the same harness configurations. For each window, eight rollouts begin from independent copies of the same parent bank. They write all chunks, are examined with reward questions, and receive per-chunk scores. The highest-scoring final bank is promoted to the next window in the same sequence. This is on-policy at two levels: tokens are sampled from the current writer, and future prompts are generated from banks produced by that writer.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Reward Construction: From Failure Surfaces to Attributed Feedback</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Why benchmark questions are not enough</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using only final questions from a long-memory benchmark creates a low-density learning problem. A long interaction sequence may contain hundreds of useful facts but only a few questions. An unasked write receives no evidence, and a failed answer does not identify whether the cause was omission, bad wording, stale-state confusion, retrieval failure, or reader failure. Binary exact match further collapses semantically partial answers and can eliminate variance within a small GRPO group <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. We construct reward items from the failure surface of memory writing, not merely from a list of benchmark answers.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Chronological segmentation</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Interaction sequences retain session boundaries and chronological order. Each session is segmented independently into chunks of roughly ten turns, so a chunk never crosses a session boundary. The resulting chunks are flattened into one chronological stream; up to five consecutive chunks form one RL window, which may span sessions. Windows from the same sequence are consumed in order, and the selected policy-written bank from one window initializes the next. This preserves long-range state transitions while keeping each optimization step bounded.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Two annotation passes</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Local write quality and long-range memory utility require different context, so the two reward types are annotated in separate passes (Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Two annotation passes ‣ 5 Reward Construction: From Failure Surfaces to Attributed Feedback ‣ Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T3" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S5.T3.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S5.T3.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T3.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.4pt 4.0pt;">
<span id="S5.T3.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:62.6pt;">
<span id="S5.T3.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Pass</span>
</span></th>
<th id="S5.T3.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.4pt 4.0pt;">

</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>The two annotation passes and the reward each one feeds.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Why the PRM pass sees the two preceding chunks.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A per-chunk probe must test information that chunk <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> itself introduced. Annotating chunk <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> in isolation fails in two ways. <em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Coreference:</em> mentions such as “that project” or “the same reviewer” cannot be resolved, so the annotator cannot write self-contained questions about them. <em id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Novelty:</em> the annotator cannot tell whether a statement is new in chunk <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> or repeats something already established, so probes would credit chunk <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> for facts it did not introduce. The extracted facts of chunks <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t{-}1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t{-}1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t{-}2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t{-}2</annotation></semantics></math> supply the referents and the recently established state. They are given as facts rather than raw text and serve as context only: no probe is generated from them, and they earn no credit for chunk <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Why not the full history.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Dependencies that span more than a few chunks are covered by the cross-chunk outcome pass, so the PRM pass does not need the whole sequence. Full history also lowers annotation quality. In a controlled comparison on identical chunks, full-history annotation used 33 times more input tokens, while the two-chunk context produced 25% more proper nouns and 59% more numbers per extracted fact. With the full sequence in view, the annotator’s attention spreads away from the current chunk and its facts become more generic, which is the over-generalization failure (Section <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Failure-surface taxonomy ‣ 5 Reward Construction: From Failure Surfaces to Attributed Feedback ‣ Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a>) that probes are meant to detect.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.22196v1/fig2_data_pipeline.svg" id="S5.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:628/282;" width="628" height="282"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Construction of the Memory RL reward artifact. Each session is split independently into chunks of about ten turns, so chunks never cross session boundaries. The chronological chunk stream is then grouped into RL windows of at most five chunks; a window may span sessions. The per-chunk probe pass writes the PRM items for chunk <math id="S5.F2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. It reads the full text of chunk <math id="S5.F2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> plus the extracted facts of chunks <math id="S5.F2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t{-}1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t{-}1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.F2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t{-}2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t{-}2</annotation></semantics></math>, used only to resolve references and decide what is new. The cross-chunk outcome pass writes ORM items from the facts of the whole window and earlier history. Structural filters and a synthetic-answer discriminability test produce the final artifact. The bottom row lists the rules that keep answer information out of the reward path (Section <a href="#S5.SS6" title="5.6 Rubrics and gold-fact attribution ‣ 5 Reward Construction: From Failure Surfaces to Attributed Feedback ‣ Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.6</span></a>).</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Failure-surface taxonomy</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5.4 Failure-surface taxonomy ‣ 5 Reward Construction: From Failure Surfaces to Attributed Feedback ‣ Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> lists the local failure modes. Cross-chunk questions add transition, coexistence, temporal, aggregation, multi-hop, and negative recall. This follows the capability decomposition exposed by LoCoMo and LongMemEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maharana et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, but the questions are generated during reward construction rather than copied from those benchmarks.</p>
</div>

<span id="S5.T4.2.8.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Content, not meta</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.2.8.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="S5.T4.2.8.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S5.T4.2.8.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">The memory stores the fact, not a meta-summary of it</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T4.2.9" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S5.T4.2.9.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="S5.T4.2.9.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:86.8pt;">
<span id="S5.T4.2.9.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Casual detail</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.2.9.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.6pt 5.0pt;">
<span id="S5.T4.2.9.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S5.T4.2.9.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">Informal but durable personal information is retained</span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Per-chunk failure-surface probes.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>Trap probes and the precision–recall trade-off</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recall alone makes “store everything” attractive. We add trap probes about content that should not have entered long-term memory, such as an assistant’s generic encouragement. Their reference answer is that the bank contains no such record. If the writer stores the irrelevant statement, retrieval exposes it and the answer becomes incorrect. Traps and the bank-growth penalty are complementary. A size penalty discourages indiscriminate volume, while traps directly test semantic selectivity. A model cannot avoid the trap merely by compressing irrelevant text into a shorter entry.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.6 </span>Rubrics and gold-fact attribution</h3>

<div id="S5.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each probe and outcome question contains weighted credit points with semantic equivalents; explicit full-, partial-, and zero-credit bands; named distractors, including stale or superseded values; evidence chunk ids; and, for outcome questions, the source facts introduced by each evidence chunk. The answer judge performs semantic matching; code only aggregates returned credit.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Gold facts are visible only to the outcome judge. They are not inserted into the bank, retrieval query, or answer-model prompt. Facts from earlier windows may provide context but are marked history-only and cannot generate credit for a current chunk.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.7 </span>Data verification</h3>

<div id="S5.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reward data must be tested as an instrument, not accepted because it is well-formed JSON. Four layers are enforced. <em id="S5.SS7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Schema validity</em> removes records with missing fields, unnormalized weights, illegal evidence ids, or illegal grading bands. <em id="S5.SS7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Causal locality</em> requires per-chunk probes to refer to the current chunk and cross-chunk questions to contain multi-chunk evidence when required. <em id="S5.SS7.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Rubric independence</em> checks that credit points do not entail one another and that distractors represent real failure modes. <em id="S5.SS7.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Discriminability</em> checks that the judge scores five synthetic answers per item in the expected order: reference and paraphrase receive full credit, a partial answer receives partial credit, and a distractor or refusal receives zero credit. In the pilot, faithful paraphrases retain an average score of 0.90.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The structural pass keeps approximately 410k of 478k generated probes and 61k of 72k generated cross-chunk questions. To control judge cost, at most three positive probes and one trap are retained per chunk. The final artifact contains 164,576 positive probes, 8,599 traps, approximately 60.8k outcome questions, and 222,395 chunk-level gold-fact references.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS7.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Future work includes a random human audit with error categories and inter-annotator agreement; a train/evaluation near-duplicate and sequence-level leakage audit; per-scenario and per-failure-type calibration on strong and weak writers; and judge sensitivity to prompt, model, and repeated sampling.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.8 </span>Harness-level artifact statistics</h3>

<div id="S5.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each complete interaction sequence is assigned to one harness configuration (Table <a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 5.8 Harness-level artifact statistics ‣ 5 Reward Construction: From Failure Surfaces to Attributed Feedback ‣ Hy-Memory-30B-A3B: Attributed Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Memory Writing" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). The offline schedule preserves within-sequence window order and consumes every row exactly twice over two epochs.</p>
</div>
